input:
This chapter covers the operation of the plate heat exchanger in its entirety, from the first fill to the final drain at the end of the run. Throughout the chapter, you, the operator, are addressed directly: the actions are your actions, presented as instructions, and the checks are your checks, to be carried out at the plate pack itself and at the instruments serving it.

Start-up

Before any flow is admitted to the unit, you should confirm that the plate pack has been correctly tightened and that the frame is showing no signs of distortion, that the gaskets are properly seated along their full length, and that the connections to the unit have been made up and adequately supported. The vents on both circuits should be opened. You should then line up the valves so that each circuit can be filled without flow being sent backwards through equipment that stands idle. The cold circuit should be filled first, and filled slowly, with venting continued until such time as liquid runs clear of air at the vent; it should be appreciated that a plate exchanger which is filled too quickly will trap air in the upper channels, and that any air so trapped will leave a portion of the surface effectively dry once the unit is in service. The hot circuit should be filled in exactly the same manner. While the unit is still cold and at low pressure, the pack edge and every connection should be carefully examined for any signs of leakage, bearing in mind that a gasket which weeps when cold is most unlikely to seal any better when hot. The hot stream should then be admitted gradually, with the outlet temperatures being watched closely as they rise. Both flows should be brought up to their duty values in a series of steps, with checks being made between steps to ensure that the pressures are steady and that no connection has started to weep as the plates expand. The exchanger can be regarded as being properly in service once the outlet temperatures are holding steady at the operating point and the pack is completely dry along its edges.

Normal operation

During normal operation, the flows should be held at the values required by the process, and the unit should be read as a whole, taking in the inlet and outlet temperatures on both sides, the pressure drop across the pack, and the general state of the gaskets at the edges. Readings should be recorded at whatever interval is laid down by the plant logging routine, since it is the record, rather than any single reading, that reveals the condition of the unit. A pressure drop that is rising whilst the flow remains unchanged indicates either that the channels are becoming fouled or that a gasket has become displaced into a port. Similarly, a temperature approach that is falling at unchanged flows indicates that the surface is losing its effectiveness, whether through fouling, through maldistribution, or through air that has found its way in with one of the streams. On no account should an attempt be made to chase a temperature deviation by forcing a flow beyond the duty of the unit, because the plate pack is a pressure boundary just as much as it is a heat-transfer surface, and its limits continue to stand regardless of the demands that the process may place upon it. The strainers on the inlet lines should be kept in service and cleaned in accordance with the routine laid down by the plant; a plate channel is a narrow passage, and solids that pass the strainer will lodge in the channels and can only be removed by opening the pack. Where the fluids involved are hazardous in nature, any weepage at the pack edge should be treated as a leak that is to be reported immediately, rather than as a minor defect that can simply be wiped away and kept under observation.

Alarms

The unit is served by two alarms. The high-temperature alarm on the hot outlet requires that the hot stream be checked: you should confirm that the cold flow is standing at its duty value, since a hot outlet temperature that is rising whilst the cold flow is falling points to a flow fault rather than to a surface fault. If the cold flow is in fact correct, the hot inlet flow should be reduced in steps until the temperature has returned within its limit, and the reduction should be reported; the unit will then be delivering less duty than the process asks for, and that shortfall belongs on the record. The high differential-pressure alarm across the pack requires that the flow be reduced and that the pack be taken out of service for inspection at the next opportunity that the process permits: a pressure drop which has climbed as far as the alarm point is stating that the channels have become obstructed, and any attempt to drive the flow against the obstruction places both the gaskets and the plates at risk. Neither alarm should simply be silenced so that operation can continue at the same duty. An alarm which repeats itself after the appropriate action has been taken amounts to a defect report, and the unit should remain at the reduced condition until such time as the underlying cause has been found.

Shutdown

When shutting down, the hot stream should be stopped first, and the cold stream should be kept flowing whilst the unit cools down; in this way the cold flow carries the stored heat out of the pack and prevents a hot, stagnant charge from standing against the gaskets. Once the outlet temperatures have fallen as far as the cold inlet temperature, the cold flow can be stopped. The unit should then be isolated on both circuits, vented, and drained down completely on both sides, because liquid that is left standing in the channels will attack the gaskets and will dry out into deposits that the next start-up will simply inherit. If the pack is to be opened, the tie bolts should be released evenly, in small steps around the frame, so that the pressure plate travels squarely and no plate is sprung. A unit that is to stand idle should be left drained, vented, and isolated, with its state properly recorded, so that the next start-up can begin from a condition that is known.
